channel.title: Eight Miles West
channel.description: The Krewson family's four centuries in America — Croesen, Kroesen, Kroessen, Kreuso, Cruse, Krewson — from a cooper who landed at Breuckelen around 1660, through Staten Island, Bucks County, Ohio, Iowa and the Pacific. Non-fiction, read from the family's own record and the colonial church books, published a chapter at a time by Michael V. Krewson.

item.title: Should Not Have Come Off Alive
item.description: The flag over Gowanus changed twice in the 1660s and 1670s and Garret Croesen never moved an inch. What moved was the family around him — a feud with the miller next door that ran ten years, from a punch in 1669 to a bloody Sunday in a grape arbour in 1679; a patent for 172 acres on Staten Island, taken the same day as his brother-in-law's, under an English governor; and then, six months after the grapes, a one-line entry in a minister's list of communicants: died 7th March 1680. His will burned. His widow sold the farm to the neighbour's family and married the other neighbour. His eldest son, eighteen, crossed the Kill.

item.title: The Name Came From Her
item.description: The family's other immigrant was not Dutch. Jan Pietersen came from Husum, on the North Sea coast of Schleswig, arrived in New Amsterdam around 1637 with a wife named Elsje, and made a living from timber, tobacco, cattle and a small yacht — signing everything with an X. Elsje is named in exactly one record in her life. Then she died, and her sons began calling themselves Staats. This is the chapter about the woman whose name the family carried and whose own name nobody wrote down.

item.title: Two Strangers Walk Across Staten Island
item.description: Six weeks after the fight in the grape arbour, two Dutchmen were rowed across from Gowanus at dawn and spent three days walking the length of Staten Island, writing down everything — the cross Englishwoman who would not show them the road, the seven houses of the Oude Dorp with three still lived in, a sick man in a brush shelter in the woods, a seventy-year-old Frenchman who leaped for joy at the sound of his own language. Their journal is the only eyewitness account of the island in the year the family took its land there. This chapter walks it with them, and then follows Derrick onto it.

item.title: The Voorlezer's Hand
item.description: Of Garret's two sons, one could write and one could not. The one who could became the first Voorlezer of the Staten Island church — bell-ringer, schoolmaster, keeper of the records — and lived in a small house built for the purpose that is now the oldest schoolhouse standing in America. Nobody knew his name for more than a century and a half, until a minister noticed that whoever kept the baptismal book had written, of one child, "my daughter." The witness at that baptism was his brother. The next year the two of them were in front of the Governor over their father's burned will.

item.title: Six Hundred Pounds of Lawful Silver
item.description: In November 1712 Derrick Kroesen, who could not write, paid six hundred pounds of Pennsylvania silver for the farm his daughter had died on and put his mark on a deed that begins at a Spanish oak. The family's next hundred years happen inside its lines. This chapter is the deeds — 580 acres, then 500 more, then the gifts to the children — and the will Derrick made in 1729, which leaves his eldest son his gold and silver buttons and one cow, makes his widow's income depend on the life of "my Negro man Fortune," and is the first place a person the family owned is named. It ends with a stone house and a date stone carved with a dead man's name.

item.title: Two Witnesses at the Font
item.description: On 5 July 1662 a baby named Elizabeth Cregier was baptized in the Reformed Dutch Church of New Amsterdam. The two men who stood as her witnesses were her grandfathers — the city's Burgomaster and the colony's Schout-Fiscal. Twenty-six months later both of them signed the surrender of New Netherland to the English. This is where the family's American story begins: not with the cooper, but with the girl his son would marry, born at the top of a world that was about to end.

item.title: The Tree Thief of Breuckelen
item.description: In March 1662 a twenty-two-year-old cooper from Winschoten went into the woods on a day of prayer and came home with some fruit trees. Within weeks the village of Breuckelen was calling Garret Dircksen Croesen a tree-thief, his minister had barred him from communion, and Garret had done the one thing nobody did in 1662 — he had the minister summoned to court. The consistory record of what followed runs ten pages, and it is the first time the family's founder speaks.
